pars.text: As is well enough known, the term φύσις in Empedocles Fr. 8 (DK) is cited by Aristotle in the *Metaphysics* (Δ 4,1014b36-1015a3) as meaning the οὐσία of natural things, in the sense of the stable substance or form that is the terminus of generation (a10-11). This interpretation is rejected almost unanimously by commentators. The three or four attempts to defend it have not proved convincing. The case now seems officially closed. Yet there remain some loose ends. These are of the kind that would keep bothering television detectives and would cause enough loss of sleep to prompt a fresh investigation of a whole case. Is that procedure called for here?

The four-line fragment of Empedocles in its entirety is taken from two quoting sources. One is Plutarch (Adv. Colot., 10; p. 1111F), who explains (1112AB) its term φύσις as γένεσις in direct contrast to "death" in the second line of the fragment. This makes it mean "birth". The other quoting source is Aetius through the pseudoPlutarchean Placita (1, 30, 1; Diels Dox., 326.14-21). No explanation of the term accompanies it. Two and a half of the four lines are quoted by Aristotle in the passage of the *Metaphysics* just noted, one and a half at GC, 11,314b7-8, and one line at GC, II 6,333b14-15. Other incomplete citations of it are extant. Of these the most important is in the pseudo Aristotelian MXG, 2,975b7, where its topic is presented as γένεσις, yet in a context in which generable things are being distinguished from eternal, and with wording that couples aorist (975a37) and perfect (b6) forms with the present.

As might be expected in these scattered sources, there are a number of textual variants. Only one (brotois in the last line, accepted from Aëthius by Bollack in his text) causes difference in today's reconstruction of the fragment. Except for that one variant in the fourth line, we may say then that a standard text has received general acceptance. In Kathleen Freeman's translation, with φύσις rendered "creation of substance" in line one, and "substance" in line four, it reads: And I shall tell you another thing: there is no creation of substance in any one of mortal existences, nor any end in execrable death, but only mixing and exchange of what has been mixed: and the name 'substance' (φύσις) is applied to them by mankind.

An implied contrast of φύσις with "death" in these lines naturally suggests the translation "birth" at least when the fragment is read in isolation. This sense for φύσις is etymologically acceptable and can claim adequate support from popular use. Burnet remarked that all commentators, including himself, had up to that time followed Plutarch in taking φύσις to mean "birth" in the fragment. Guthrie, briefly surveying the situation, concludes that Plutarch's γένεσις is the only meaning that "makes good sense of the passage", and accordingly translates φύσις in both places in the fragment as "birth". Kahn, also endorsing Plutarch's understanding of φύσις in the quotation, states this side of the discussion even more strongly: "The various modern attempts to justify Aristotle's interpretation all make nonsense of Empedocles' verse". Aristotle, in consequence, either misunderstands φύσις in the fragment (DK 31B 8, ad Joe.), or "interprets the word in both ways" (Guthrie, II, 140, n. 1), or draws out for his own purposes a meaning that Empedocles did not explicitly put into the term. A parallel situation in Anaxagoras' (DK 59B 17) rejection of γίγνεσθαι, moreover, may be used to illustrate Empedocles' denial of φύσις.

On the other side of the dispute, Lovejoy (p. 371) noted that Empedocles (Fr. 17.3) positively asserted the genesis of mortal things in the sense of their birth. Using φύσις in a way similar to Democritus, Empedocles in virtue of his own philosophy "may naturally have said that only the elements --not 'mortal things'-- possess a real φύσις" (p. 372). Secondly, Lovejoy (pp. 373-383) showed that in literary use, in Presocratic philosophy, and in its adverbial use in the dative, the "dominant and central sense" (p. 376) of φύσις down through the fifth century was "nature". However, he added, in support of his view, that the second line of Empedocles Fr. 6 may mean no "end of death", that is, that death will always take place. This weak point was sharply attacked, thereby drawing attention away from the two main reasons just noted.

Burnet, changing his own earlier view, accepted Lovejoy's reasoning that for Empedocles no mortal thing can have "ultimate reality" (p. 206, n. 4) if only the four elements have a φύσις that does not pass away. Ross, while cautiously acknowledging that Lovejoy's argument is "not conclusive", regards the opinion it supports as "the more probable", and Burnet's translation "substance" as more likely to be correct. He uses "nature" in the Oxford translation.

Finally, Gustav A. Seeck gives a complicated explanation. Aristotle, he maintains, thinks first of all of the sense of φύσις as genesis in the list of its meanings. GC 314b5-6 and 333b13 ff. attribute, in Seeck's opinion, that meaning of genesis to the term in the Empedoclean lines. In the *Metaphysics*, Seeck finds no change of view on Aristotle's part. Rather, the passage in the *Metaphysics* makes the lines from Empedocles bear on the mixture and exchange, which Aristotle takes in the sense of οὐσία as matter but then goes on to include the implication of οὐσία in its primary sense of form. Accordingly Seeck (p. 40) claims to be confirming through Aristotle the usually accepted interpretation of φύσις as genesis in Empedocles Fr. 8, with Aristotle not intending to explain the meaning in Empedocles but merely to illustrate his own thought.

The loose ends that cause trouble should be apparent enough from this brief survey of the controversy. First, if the alleged contrast of φύσις with "death" in the fragment --the main argument from Plutarch on-- so obviously pinpoints the meaning to "birth", how could Aristotle ever have missed anything so patent? He had just listed genesis as the first sense of φύσις. It would still be vivid in his mind. He could hardly fail to see it in the fragment if the supposed contrast with death determined the meaning. One becomes suspicious that something deeper may be at stake.

Secondly, the use of φύσις for birth or growth does not seem to be usual in other philosophical fragments of the time. Empedocles might of course be the first to introduce it into this area from one of the popular uses. If he were the first, the reasons for the innovation should be probed. But the presumption, in point of historical situation, seems the opposite. The ἐστί at the beginning of the fourth line in the fragment appears to be emphatic and to be set in contrast to naming, along the lines of the Parmenidean being and seeming. This chronological background would suggest rather the overall meaning that mortal things seem to have a special nature of their own but do not.

Thirdly, could Aristotle, as Seeck suggests, have taken genesis as the meaning at first glance, and afterwards proceed to draw in his own thought the conclusion that the notion thereby denied by Empedocles was "stable nature"? If this be so, Aristotle is not misunderstanding Empedocles if the original meaning of φύσις in the fragment is genesis. He would merely be explaining the term from his own viewpoint in a way that implies the denial by Empedocles of a formal nature for mortal things. Yet why would he not have dealt with the fragment under the first sense he had listed for φύσις, a sense explicitly acknowledged as genesis?

Three questions, accordingly, call for answers. They correspond to the three loose ends just noted. First, what exactly did Aristotle himself understand by οὐσία in thinking that it was the φύσις denied by Empedocles in the fragment? Secondly, what did Empedocles mean by φύσις when he wrote those lines? Thirdly, would it have made any difference to Aristotle's explanation whether Empedocles had meant stable nature or dynamic process by the term φύσις in those verses?

When quoting Empedocles Fr. 8 in the *Metaphysics* (Δ4,1014b16-1015a19), Aristotle had listed first the dynamic sense of φύσις as genesis, then its static senses of source of primary motion, of a thing's primary material, and of the substance of natural things understood as their form. Among the examples of primary material taken by other thinkers to be nature he groups fire, earth, air and water, the four "roots" of things for Empedocles (Fr. 6) and later known as the four Empedoclean elements. But it is not this sense of nature he finds denied in the Empedoclean fragment 8. What he finds rejected in the fragment is nature meaning form in the sense of substance, the form that is the *terminus* of generation (1015b1-11). The description is plain and explicit, and is given in the terms regularly used in the *Physics* and *Metaphysics*. It is clearly his own notion of form in the category of substance that he finds denied by Empedocles in the statement that there is no φύσις of any of existent things.

But how could Aristotle have expected to find in Empedocles any inkling of form in the category of substance? The answer seems given quite clearly in the first Book of the *Metaphysics* (A 10,993a15-24). There Aristotle asserted that the early philosophy spoke in a halting way about everything. As an instance, he mentions that Empedocles held bone to exist by virtue of its λόγος. But this, Aristotle states, is the form or οὐσία of the thing. The reference seems to be to the proportion of earth, water and fire in the composition of bone, as in Empedocles Fr. 96. He then argues that if someone else had explained this notion of οὐσία to Empedocles the latter would have agreed on its extension to all things: *But it is similarly necessary that flesh and each of the other tissues should be the ratio of its elements, or that not one of them should; for it is on account of this that both flesh and bone and everything else will exist, and not on account of the matter, which he names, --fire and earth and water and air. But while he would necessarily have agreed if another had said this, he has not said it clearly*.

Aristotle, then, classes Empedocles' "proportion" under his own "form", and the four Empedoclean "roots" as "matter", expressed very obscurely. While admitting form in this way for one thing, namely bone, Aristotle accuses Empedocles of inconsistently denying it in other things, and really holding that other things exist on account of their matter. It is in this sense that he can find the denial of οὐσία in the formal signification extending to all mortal things in Fr. 8.

Aristotle again cites a line and a half of Empedocles Fr. 8 at GC 11, 314b7-8. There he is arguing that pluralists such as Empedocles have to distinguish alteration from genesis, and that Empedocles speaks in this way in saying "there is no φύσις of anything". That remark would be odd if Aristotle were taking φύσις in the fragment to mean genesis. He speaks (314b8-26) as though these thinkers admit genesis as understood in their own way, but cannot be consistent when they distinguish alteration from it. The reason is that the Empedoclean elements are differentiated by their respective qualities, and "since it is not possible for Fire to become Water, or Water to Become Earth, neither will it be possible for anything white to become black, or anything soft to become hard" (b23-25).

The reasoning of Aristotle in this passage, then, is that if no οὐσία (b14) distinct from qualities is admitted, alteration cannot be distinguished from genesis. Yet these pluralists admit no φύσις in sense of οὐσία, but only "mixing and exchange of what was mixed", in which alteration cannot be rendered discernible from what they call genesis. The point is that they in their own words acknowledge genesis, but have no means of consistently distinguishing alteration from it. For the sequence of his reasoning, Aristotle has to be understanding φύσις here in the sense of οὐσία, its differentiating function serving to pinpoint it for his immediate purpose to οὐσία as form. Yet Lovejoy (p. 373) finds that the context here does not establish the meaning of φύσις "with absolute certainty", and other commentators, for instance Joachim (p.67) and Guthrie (II, 140, n.1) conclude that Aristotle is understanding it in the sense of genesis. The text itself has to be the last court of appeal. In it genesis (314b6; 315a5-8; a18; a22-23) is conceded to Empedocles, with φύσις restricted for him to the ungenerated elements. Does not that make definite enough the understanding of φύσις as stable nature, in contradistinction to genesis, in this Aristotelian text?

The Empedoclean fragment is cited a third time --on this occasion one line only-- at GC, II 6,333b14. At issue is the uniformity in natural genesis, why man comes from man and wheat from wheat. Similarly bone has to come to be by a certain λόγος. The cause of this uniformity is "the οὐσία of each thing, and not only 'mixing and exchange of what was mixed'". That cause makes a natural thing be of a definite kind, and is its φύσις (b3-18). What the "mixing and exchange" had been contrasted with in the fragment was φύσις, and now Aristotle expresses that contrasted term as οὐσία explained in the sense of form. There can be no doubt that what he read in the verses as φύσις he is here understanding as form in the category of substance, just as when he quotes the fragment in the *Metaphysics*.

In all three passages in which he quotes the fragment, then, Aristotle is understanding the term φύσις in it to mean the substantial nature of things, in the sense of their formal cause in his own explanation of their nature. It is this φύσις that he finds Empedocles denying in the assertion that there is no nature in any existent thing, even though Empedocles knew of it only vaguely and could speak of it only in lisping fashion. He seems to allow Empedocles the right to use the term genesis (cf. Fr.9) in the sense of mixing and exchange, in arguing that so understood it does not allow alteration to be distinguished from it. With our reading "there is no nature of any one of mortals", of course, Aristotle's reasoning falls easily enough into focus. With his own transmitted reading "of any one of existent things", the four Empedoclean elements have to be kept on the side of matter, which does not become actually an existent thing until it receives its form. What functions as absolutely primitive matter should not from Aristotle's viewpoint have a nature of its own in the sense under discussion. The relevant point, however, is that in all three citations Aristotle understands φύσις to mean stable nature in the fragment.

A different question, however, is what Empedocles himself meant by φύσις in the fragment. If the passage is taken just by itself, does it not read naturally enough with φύσις understood as birth or growth? The meaning would be: "There is no birth of any mortal, nor death, but only mixing and exchange of what was mixed". Death of something mortal would not sound any more incongruous in Greek (τελευτή - θνητός) than in English, since in neither case does the same root enter into the two words used. The notion could be proposed and denied without giving the appearance of dismissing an immediately evident contradiction. Φύσις in this sense of genesis could be readily denied to the order of reality and limited entirely to the realm of naming and seeming.

On the other hand, the philosophical use and the more common literary use of the term φύσις at the time was in the sense of a stable characterization. Does not this use also give a good sense in the fragment even when taken by itself? Lack of stable nature in all mortals would exemplify neatly enough an overall Empedoclean tenet, namely that what exists can never perish (Fr. 12). Mortals, though, do perish. Accordingly they can have no φύσις, in the sense of any stable being of their own. Their only being is the being of their components. In this setting, as Plutarch explains (1113D), both those not yet born and those already dead exist. As mortals, therefore, none of them adds a nature over and above the nature of the components. None of them has a φύσις of his own in this signification. Empedocles' concern was to deny the engendering of any being of which the preceding status was non-being. Genesis of a mortal nature would have been creation in the full sense of production of being from non-being, a consideration that supports Kathleen Freeman's translation of φύσις as "creation of substance".

The contrasted τελευτή lends itself even more readily to a static sense. Just as there is no mortal nature, so there is no end of anything through death. The explicit mention of "death" indicates the more general meaning of "end" for τελευτή in this verse. Death, the sense is, does not mean an end, since all that exists in the mortal thing continues in existence. The Homeric (I1., 1,297) setting in the first line of the fragment is continued in the notion of "baneful" death. As with Epicurus (Third Letter, 124-126) later on, death is nothing to be dreaded. For Empedocles, the reason is that no perishing is involved in it. The traditionally accepted notion of death is clearly what Empedocles has in view in the fragment. But what he immediately opposes to φύσις, in the construction of the fragment, is not "death" but "end". The contrast, accordingly, does not require the meaning of "birth" for φύσις.

The terms "mixing (μίξις) and exchange (διάλλαξις)" can have **a static as well as a dynamic meaning**. The one can mean the finished mixture or the process of mixing. The other can mean the exchange already accomplished or the act of exchanging, and possibly, in both senses, differentiation. The dynamic meanings would be the ones more naturally to be expected. In Empedocles' thought the one type of signification can hardly mean anything different from the other. In the world as we experience it at present the elements are in continual process under strife, and the lack of stable nature in mortal things allows designation of these objects in terms of process. The use of dynamic terms here, then, would not at all entail that φύσις in the opening line of the fragment has to be taken in the dynamic sense of birth. The dynamic term in this context permits reference to the mortal not only at the time of his birth, but also to him at any fleeting moment of his lifetime. The one aspect can easily slide into the other in the Empedoclean way of thinking, since both "birth" and "human nature" alike consist in the mixing and exchange.

But what is meant by saying that only mixing and exchange can exist? The meaning cannot be that either the birth or the stable nature of mortal things exists. Whichever way the term φύσις is taken, that is exactly what is being denied. In the overall framework of Empedocles' own thinking, the elements are what exist. They are ingenerable, unchangeable, and imperishable. In saying that the mixture of them exists, Empedocles can be allowing existence only to the elements themselves. It is far too early for multisignificant acceptations of being. The only being involved is the being of the elements, and that is the only being found in the mixture. Any notion that the mixing adds a new and accidental type of being would obviously be too Aristotelian to be expected in Empedocles himself.

Finally, there is the concluding sentence in the fragment. It is often understood as "φύσις is a name given them by men". Whether φύσις is understood as "birth" or as "stable nature", the sentence then means that the formation of man (or of horse, oak, and so on) belongs only to the world of seeming, the world set up by human convention. Φύσις is a name given to mortal things or to the mixing and separation of their elements, according as it is interpreted in a static or in a dynamic sense. But a *tmesis* construction is also possible in the sentence. Φύσις then becomes a nominative predicate. The sentence now reads: "And it is called φύσις by men". The "it" would refer back to what was wrongly introduced as φύσις in the opening line of the fragment, and expressed as "mixing and exchange" in the third line. The overall meaning remains practically the same. But the notion that the real world is what is being "named" by men is brought out more vividly, in accord with the quite evident Parmenidean background of Empedocles' thinking.

Having examined the different parts of the fragment as it stands today, one is now faced directly with the question how φύσις in its lines would have been understood by Empedocles and his contemporary readers or listeners. Empedocles' concern was to show that only the unchangeable elements existed in the world, and that the rest was "naming" or construction by human cognition. Would the meaning of "birth" for φύσις satisfy this purpose? Yes. He expresses the general notion elsewhere (frs. 9, 11, 12, 17,23) from the viewpoint of production and generation, though without using the term φύσις in this regard. On the other hand the notion of stable specification and differentiation would do just as well in the context. Empedocles had no interest in making the Aristotelian distinction between generation as a way to substantial form, and substantial form in completed actuality. The global notion that mortal things acquire and have being of their own was what he meant to deny.

The prevalent use of φύσις at the time in the sense of stable nature in philosophical literature may give some preference for the static sense of the word in the fragment. But it is not decisive. Also there may have been something in the immediate context that led Plutarch to introduce the fragment in a setting (1111E) in which φύσις, like "animal" and "soul", had a static meaning. Plutarch (1112A) himself claims that Empedocles here means "birth", on the ground that he is contrasting it with death. But Plutarch goes on (1112D-1113B) to discuss both φύσις and genesis in the sense of the things born or generated, in which "the nature of Colotes" is Colotes himself. Is he aware of something in the immediate context that might be responsible for Aristotle's attitude in passing by the sense of "birth" and focusing upon "substance", in his understanding of φύσις in the fragment? Again, the indications are not decisive. But all in all, the evidence seems to swing the balance, even though but slightly, in favor of the static notion of the term in Empedocles' mind as he composed the four lines of the fragment. He was merely stressing that nothing existed over and above the elements and forces. In this perspective neither Aristotelian meaning --substance, or change specified by substance-- was contrasted with the other.

Finally, in answer to the third of the proposed questions, would it have made any difference to Aristotle whether or not Empedocles was using φύσις in the static sense? Doctrinally, generation for Aristotle was the way to form in the category of substance, and was specified by substantial form. Without the notion of substantial form, there could be for him no philosophical concept of generation. If Empedocles in global fashion was denying birth, without consideration for Aristotelian technicalities, he was thereby denying substance in the sense of form. Empedocles was not denying process, he was not denying mixture and differentiation. All that he was denying was, for Aristotle, process specified by substantial form. The key notion denied was thereby that of substance. Would not this be enough to allow Aristotle to say that the use of the term φύσις in the citation was that of "substance", even though he had been fully aware that its immediate meaning in the context was "birth"?

Hardly. That way of assessing the situation might have been acceptable if Aristotle had not just passed by the meaning of φύσις as "the genesis of growing things" (Metaph., Δ4, 1014b16) as the first in his listing of its significations. If he were thinking on the basis that in its original context the Empedoclean φύσις was indifferent to the two meanings, he could scarcely have come out so decisively for it as an illustration of the static meaning "substance". It would not be an instance of its use that contradistinguished it immediately and vividly from the use in the meaning of "birth" just mentioned. Aristotle had to be understanding the word as having a static sense in the fragment, in the line of being rather than of becoming. There is no sign that he is reading it in one sense and then reasoning to another sense in order to make his point. Rather, his presentation of the fragment indicates that in it he read φύσις to mean a stable nature that radically distinguished one mortal thing from another, and for him this was nothing other than form in the category of substance. Only from the angle that he takes it in reference to all generable things, while Empedocles perhaps was thinking only of "mortal men", is there room for a charge of misinterpretation.

The results of this inquiry suggest, then, that Aristotle consistently understands φύσις to mean stable nature in the category of substance, on all three occasions on which he cites the Empedoclean lines. He finds the sense, the inquiry indicates, to be the one put into the lines by their author, in a stammering way, of course, but open to expression in Aristotelian terms. As to the further problem whether Aristotle is mistaken about the force of the term in Empedocles, a decisive answer is hardly possible. But the prevailing use of the term φύσις in the philosophical literature of the epoch, and Plutarch's discussion of it against a background in which it meant being, tend to tip the scales somewhat in favor of the correctness of Aristotle's view. In any case, Aristotle's procedure requires that the static meaning was the one he himself saw in the Empedoclean lines. It does not allow the assumption that he found in them first of all the dynamic meaning, and then by further reasoning built up a case for the sense of φύσις as form in the category of substance.

Rather, the interest in the whole topic lies in the vivid confrontation of one type of thought with another. **Aristotle's penetrating philosophy had come to see in living things something more than both the matter of which they were composed and the influences of their efficient causes**. Here in Empedocles he was confronted with a way of thinking that saw in mortal things no other reality than the component elements and the work of love and strife. What would be the first and most glaring *lacuna* he would note in this confrontation? Could it be anything other than the lack of form in the category of substance? An explicit denial of substantial form was quite to be awaited. Empedocles (Fr. 17.3) did not deny the birth of mortal things. Aristotle could hardly be looking for so obviously an anti-motherhood statement in the verses. What Empedocles could be expected to be denying was any further reality over and above the elements and forces. That, for Aristotle, was φύσις in the sense of substance as form. Accordingly, from his own viewpoint, he is correctly understanding the meaning of φύσις in Empedocles Fr. 6. A case may be made that in writing the lines Empedocles himself was thinking of "birth". But even if so, the indications show definitely enough that what he was thereby intent on denying to men was a special nature of their own.
